title: Interest, forbidden
hookLine: interest is forbidden (2:275), and the reasons scholars give

lines: TRADE IS JUST LIKE RIBA, THEY SAY.
cards: Yesterday the market was praised. Today the Qur'an draws a hard line through it. In surah two, it describes people who say trade is just like riba, just like charging interest.
Both are deals, both make money; what's the difference? The verse answers without arguing, in Pickthall's words: "Allah permitteth trading and forbiddeth usury."
Two things that look alike on a spreadsheet, one allowed and one forbidden. The passage calls believers to give up what remains owed to them of riba, and warns those who won't.

teach.h: RIBA: GAIN ON A LOAN, FOR TIME.
teach.b: Pickthall renders riba as usury; it's also called interest: an extra amount charged on a loan just because time has passed. The Qur'an ties it to growth.

In surah thirty, what you give in riba so that it may grow on other people's wealth does not grow with God, while what you give in charity does. Two kinds of increase, pointed opposite ways. The hadith sharpen the line.

teach.h: THE ONE WHO PAYS, WRITES, WITNESSES.
teach.b: In Sahih Muslim, Jabir reports that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ cursed the one who consumes riba, the one who pays it, the one who writes it down and the two witnesses, and said they are all alike.
The whole transaction, not only the lender. Why?
The Qur'an gives one reason in the same passage: if you repent, you keep your capital, and you neither wrong nor are wronged. Scholars built on that.

teach.h: NEED, RISK, AND WHO GETS RICHER.
teach.b: Some point to need: the borrower is often the one in trouble, and interest lets the strong profit from the weak one's bad season.
Some point to risk: in trade both sides can win or lose, but a fixed interest payment lets the lender gain whatever happens to the borrower.
Some point to the community: the Qur'an elsewhere warns against wealth circulating only among the rich. And how this meets today's banks is still argued.
Some fiqh councils have ruled that ordinary bank interest is riba; some individual scholars have argued otherwise. That conversation leads straight into tomorrow.

how: Muslims who keep this rule avoid paying or receiving interest, using Islamic banks, interest-free loans within families and communities, or other arrangements; scholars and fiqh councils still discuss how the rule applies to modern banking.

o: any profit made by buying and selling goods
an extra charge on a loan just for time passing
a yearly payment from savings that goes to the poor

p: riba does not grow with God

s: in the Qur'an, trade and riba are treated as the same thing
the verse quotes people who say so, and answers that God permits trade and forbids riba.
the hadith in Sahih Muslim blames only the lender
it names the one who consumes it, pays it, writes it and witnesses it.
scholars give more than one reason for the ban
need and exploitation, one-sided risk, and wealth circulating only among the rich.

games.q: you're in the crowd when the verse is recited. people have been saying: trade is just like interest. what does the verse answer?
o: it agrees, but asks for a low rate.
God permits trade and forbids riba.
it says the matter is up to each person.
games.why: the verse doesn't argue the point; it simply draws the line: trade permitted, riba forbidden.

practice: Let one debt come clearly into view, either direction: money you owe on a card, a loan or to a friend, or money or favors someone owes you.
Notice where it sits in your body when you name it, and how you hold it over them, or don't. The Qur'an asks lenders to give time to a debtor in hardship; just breathe with that for a while.

wordCard.voice: Riba. Interest or usury: a fixed gain charged on a loan, which the Qur'an forbids while it permits trade. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: usury or interest; the Qur'an contrasts it with charity as two kinds of growth.

carryVoice: Your line: no interest. A week of law at home and in the market: a wedding feast, rights both ways, a kind divorce, fair children, a third by will, the honest merchant, and now riba. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: Allah permitteth trading and forbiddeth usury.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 1598 (Jabir: the curse on all parties to riba)
